tables.heading_context: ## AC vs DC: Why Tesla Won, and Why DC Is Coming Back
rows: AC cable acts as a capacitor; capacitive charging current dominates at length → almost no real power delivered. DC has no such limit.
HVDC links two AC systems without requiring frequency synchronization. The Pacific DC Intertie (CA–OR–WA) operates without the two ends being in sync.
HVDC losses are lower than AC over very long distances, even including converter station losses (~0.6% per 100 km for DC vs ~1-2% for AC including reactive losses).
Same capacitive issue as submarine. London, NYC, urban underground systems increasingly HVDC.
Power flow in AC networks is governed by impedance ratios (Kirchhoff) — you can't easily direct where power goes. HVDC sets power flow precisely and quickly.

tables.heading_context: ## The Grid as a Distributed Real-Time System
rows: Grid frequency (60.000 Hz) — all synchronous generators must agree on this single value; it emerges from physics, not software
N-1 contingency planning — system must remain stable and serve all load despite any single component failure
Electromagnetic propagation at ~0.97c — effectively zero delay vs mechanical response time
Energy storage (pumped hydro, batteries) — the grid has almost no native buffering; storage is expensive and limited
Economic dispatch + AGC (Automatic Generation Control) — continuously allocates generation to match load
Protection relay + circuit breaker — detects fault, isolates faulted segment in < 100 ms, redistributes load
Grid can't sacrifice Consistency (frequency) or Availability (serving load) — Partition tolerance managed by DC tie isolation
Frequency restoration via AGC — after a disturbance, returns to exactly 60.000 Hz within minutes, not immediately
Grid cascade — one line trip overloads neighbors, exponential cascade; 2003 Northeast Blackout, 55M people
Microgrid islanding — local system survives external failure by disconnecting at controlled boundary
Under-frequency load shedding (UFLS) — automatically drops load to match remaining supply
PMU (Phasor Measurement Unit) measurements — GPS-synced, 30-120 samples/sec, real-time situational awareness
Transmission topology changes — must track line status in real-time for accurate power flow models
Frequency at which generators trip offline
Separate energy balance, instantaneous power balance, frequency response, voltage support, reserves, and protection action.
Annual MWh adequacy does not prove real-time operability.
Whether transmission voltage is high enough
Estimate current, I²R loss, thermal limit, voltage drop, right-of-way, and reactive-power burden.
Higher voltage lowers losses but raises insulation, clearance, equipment, and permitting cost.
Whether AC or HVDC is the right bulk-transfer architecture
Check distance, cable vs overhead, asynchronous interconnection, controllability, converter-station cost, and reliability model.
HVDC wins some long/cable/asynchronous cases; HVAC remains cheaper and simpler for many networked overhead corridors.
Compute actual MWh over nameplate MWh and then ask what hours the output arrives.
Capacity factor is not capacity credit; timing and dispatchability determine grid value.
Identify lost MW, inertia, governor response, AGC, reserves, under-frequency load shedding, and protection settings.
The same MW loss is more severe on a low-inertia or weakly connected system.
Look at net load, ramp rate, curtailment, storage duration, transmission export path, and flexible demand.
The problem is not "too much solar"; it is temporal/location mismatch plus insufficient flexibility.
Trace marginal unit, congestion, losses, scarcity adders, uplift, and local market rules.
Merit order explains the baseline; real LMPs are also network prices.
Map contingency, automatic power redistribution, relay action, voltage collapse risk, and operator time window.
Cascades are system-state dependent; N-1 planning reduces but does not eliminate correlated or hidden failures.
